prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Jenny's phone number is for sale, but not for a song. "867-5309/Jenny" originally appeared on Tommy Tutone's "Tommy Tutone 2" album. Bids for a New Jersey version of the number, stuck in the minds of millions since Tommy Tutone's "867-5309/Jenny" hit the Top 10 in 1982, had reached $5,100 on eBay as of Monday morning. The song is about a guy who finds Jenny's name and number scribbled on a bathroom wall. "This is really, in my opinion, one of the last cultural remnants of the '80s pop culture era ... other than the mullet," said Spencer Potter, a 28-year-old DJ who is selling the number he got for free five years ago. While Potter is overlooking the fact that "867-5309" is an active phone number in dozens of other area codes, it does get called a lot by curious people. Potter said he has gotten about 40 calls a day since he got the area code 201 version for his Weehawken, New Jersey, DJ business. "The minute we plugged the phone jack into the wall, it began ringing," Potter said. Mostly, Potter said, the callers are "a lot of '80s fanatics" and he lets the calls ring through to his voice mail. When he did answer a call three years ago, Potter found his own Jenny on the line. "She had been using my number to give out to guys that she didn't like at bars," he said. "It was a bum phone number." The young lady from Hoboken, New Jersey, told Potter she was just curious about who might be getting the calls. Potter ended up asking her out. "I figured if she was having to give out a bum number that often then she was probably pretty cute," he said. "We ended up meeting for drinks. We dated for awhile and it was actually a great friendship." Potter recently moved from Weehawken and decided to try to make money off the infamous digits with an eBay auction. Potter's DJ business goes with the number, a necessary provision to get around phone company rules against selling telephone numbers, he said. Phone companies technically own the numbers, not the customers. Potter said Vonage, the company that assigned the number, gave him permission to transfer it as part of the sale of his business. EBay halted a 2004 auction by the purported holder of the 212 area code version of the number, The New York Times reported. A Philadelphia-area resident who holds the toll-free versions -- both 800 and 888 -- said he values his numbers in the millions. Jeffrey Steinberg said his best offer so far, rejected several years ago, was for $1 million from a national weight-loss company. He acquired the numbers in the early 1990s for a pizza delivery campaign and has licensed them for other advertisers in the years since. Potter said when his auction ends next Monday, February 9, he hopes to make at least $40,000. He said he would use the money to take a Caribbean vacation -- away from his ringing phone. . CNN's Laurie Segall and CNN Radio's April Williams contributed to this report.

(CNN) — The telephone number made famous as Jenny’s is on the market—and the asking price is far from cheap.

Tommy Tutone’s “867-5309/Jenny,” first released on the album “Tommy Tutone 2,” became a Top 10 hit in 1982 and embedded the digits in the memories of millions. By Monday morning, bidding on eBay for a New Jersey number matching the song had climbed to $5,100.

The song tells the story of a man who discovers Jenny’s name and phone number written on a restroom wall.

Spencer Potter, the 28-year-old DJ auctioning the number, received it at no cost five years ago. He described it as, in his view, “one of the last cultural remnants” of 1980s pop culture, aside from the mullet.

Although 867-5309 remains an active number in dozens of area codes—something Potter is disregarding—the famous sequence attracts plenty of curious callers. Potter said the 201-area-code number has received roughly 40 calls per day since he began using it for his DJ company in Weehawken, New Jersey.

According to Potter, the phone started ringing as soon as it was connected. Most callers are devoted fans of the 1980s, he said, and he generally allows their calls to go to voice mail.

One time, however, answering the phone led Potter to a real-life Jenny. Three years ago, he spoke to a woman who had been giving his number to men she met in bars but did not like, believing it was a fake number.

The Hoboken, New Jersey, woman told him she wanted to find out who was actually receiving those calls. Potter eventually invited her on a date. He reasoned that if she needed to hand out a false number so frequently, she was probably attractive.

The two met for drinks, dated for a period and developed what Potter called a great friendship.

After recently leaving Weehawken, Potter decided to see whether he could profit from the well-known digits by listing them on eBay. Because telephone-company policies prohibit the direct sale of phone numbers, the auction also includes Potter’s DJ business. Technically, phone companies—not subscribers—own telephone numbers.

Potter said Vonage, which issued the number, authorized him to transfer it in connection with the business sale.

A similar auction in 2004 was stopped by eBay, according to The New York Times. That listing was posted by someone claiming to control the 212-area-code version of 867-5309.

Meanwhile, Jeffrey Steinberg, a Philadelphia-area resident who owns both the 800 and 888 toll-free versions, said he believes his numbers are worth millions of dollars. His highest offer to date was $1 million from a nationwide weight-loss company several years ago, but he turned it down.

Steinberg obtained the toll-free numbers in the early 1990s for a pizza-delivery promotion and has since licensed them to other advertisers.

Potter’s auction is scheduled to close on Monday, February 9. He hopes the sale will bring in at least $40,000, which he plans to spend on a Caribbean vacation—far from the constantly ringing telephone.

CNN’s Laurie Segall and CNN Radio’s April Williams contributed to the report.

# Decades after “Jenny,” 867-5309 is still a number worth fighting for

More than four decades after Tommy Tutone turned 867-5309 into one of pop music’s most memorable phone numbers, businesses and collectors still covet its hundreds of area-code variations.

The reason is simple: Almost anyone who hears “867-5309” can recall the melody — and many can remember the number without writing it down. For advertisers, that kind of recognition can be more valuable than a conventional “vanity” number spelling a company’s name.

The number entered popular culture with Tommy Tutone’s 1981 single “867-5309/Jenny.” Because the lyrics did not include an area code, callers began dialing the seven digits in communities across the United States and Canada. Many reached surprised homeowners, businesses or recorded messages; others heard busy signals as prank calls poured in.

Its commercial value was demonstrated years later when New Jersey disc jockey Spencer Potter offered his business — including the right to use 201-867-5309 — on eBay. Bidding reportedly climbed to about $80,000 before the listing was removed amid questions about whether a telephone number could legally be sold.

That distinction remains important. Under Federal Communications Commission and telephone-industry rules, subscribers generally do not own their numbers as personal property. Numbers are part of the North American Numbering Plan and are allocated to telephone companies, which assign them to customers. A customer normally receives a right to use a number, not a title to it.

Number portability allows customers to take a number to another carrier, but it does not turn the number into property that can be transferred like a car or a parcel of land. Carriers can reclaim disconnected numbers, and sales platforms have often barred direct auctions of telephone numbers.

Sellers have tried to work around those restrictions by transferring a business, telephone account, website or other assets with the number attached. Any such transfer can still depend on the carrier’s rules and approval, and a winning auction bid does not necessarily guarantee that the number will move successfully.

There is also no single 867-5309. Every area code creates a different full telephone number, leaving hundreds of possible “Jennys.” Over the years, versions have been held by DJs, plumbing and heating companies, real-estate agents, restaurants, radio stations and private individuals. Some holders use the number as a marketing hook; others play recordings of the song or simply endure calls from curious fans.

Toll-free and high-profile metropolitan-area versions can be especially attractive because they reach larger markets or are easier to advertise nationally. But even a local version can save a business money: Customers who already know the song may remember the company’s number after seeing its area code only once.

The number’s endurance also shows why memorable telephone numbers remain useful despite online search, social media and mobile contact lists. A web address can be forgotten, and an advertisement can disappear with a swipe. The chorus of “867-5309/Jenny,” however, has been lodged in listeners’ memories since the Reagan era.

For the people who control one of its many area-code versions, that eight-second musical memory continues to ring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
